title: Pallas et Arachne
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Minerva, having just heard the Muses out and approved their anger, turns her mind to Arachne, a Lydian weaver of humble birth whose skill has made her famous and who refuses to admit that Pallas taught her. The goddess comes to her disguised as an old woman, is insulted, throws off the disguise, and the two set up looms apart from each other. Minerva weaves the twelve gods enthroned and her own victory over Neptune in the quarrel over the naming of Cecrops' land, with four small panels in the corners showing mortals punished for challenging gods; Arachne weaves a long catalogue of the gods' disguises and the women they took under them. The work is faultless, and that is why Minerva tears it, strikes her, and — after Arachne hangs herself — leaves her alive as a spider.

advisory.lede: Arachne's tapestry is a catalogue of rape: Jupiter, Neptune, Apollo, Bacchus and Saturn taking women by force and by disguise, close to twenty assaults in some twenty-four lines.
advisory.more: The panel runs from Europa carried off by the bull through Asterie, Leda, Antiope, Alcmena, Danae, Aegina, Mnemosyne, Proserpina, Canace, Tyro, Theophane, Ceres, Medusa, Melantho, Isse and Erigone — some eighteen episodes, most of them given a line or two: the shape the god put on, and what he did in it. Several of the women are not named at all but identified only by their fathers, and the compression is part of the argument. The panel is built as an indictment, and Ovid twice breaks off to address a victim or a god directly. Lectorium presents the text unaltered, and the translations render the assaults as the Latin states them rather than smoothing them into seduction. The tale also ends with Arachne beaten about the head and hanging herself before the goddess transforms her.

sentences.t:
Praebuerat dictis Tritonia talibus aures
carminaque Aonidum iustamque probaverat iram.
sentences.l: Tritonia had lent her ears to such words, and had approved the songs of the Aonides and their just anger.
sentences.i: Tritonia had given ear to words like these, and had approved the Aonides' songs and their anger as just.
sentences.n: Tritonia is a cult title of Minerva, the goddess called Pallas throughout this part. The Aonides are the Muses, named from Aonia, the country of Mount Helicon. Both verbs are pluperfect: the listening is finished before this tale starts.

sentences.t:
Tum secum “laudare parum est; laudemur et ipsae
numina nec sperni sine poena nostra sinamus”
sentences.l: Then to herself: “to praise is too little; let us ourselves also be praised, and let us not allow our own divinity to be scorned without penalty”
sentences.i: Then to herself: “Praising is not enough; let us be praised in our own right, and let no one scorn our godhead unpunished”
sentences.n: The verb of speaking is left out after secum, as often. laudemur is a hortatory subjunctive in the passive, 'let us be praised'. The first-person plurals are the poetic plural for the singular — she is one goddess — and the feminine ipsae sets her beside the Muses she has just heard out in the opening lines: their songs were praised and their anger was just, and she means the same for herself. sino takes the infinitive: 'let us not allow to be scorned'.

sentences.t:
Maeoniaeque animum fatis intendit Arachnes,
quam sibi lanificae non cedere laudibus artis
audierat.
sentences.l: and she bent her mind to the fates of Maeonian Arachne, whom she had heard did not yield to her in the praises of the wool-working art.
sentences.i: and she turned her thoughts to the doom of Arachne of Maeonia, who, she had heard, would not concede her the honours of the weaver's craft.
sentences.n: Maeonia is Lydia, in western Asia Minor. 'fatis intendit animum' — she fixes her mind on Arachne's fate: the doom is settled before the contest is even proposed. 'quam ... non cedere ... audierat' is an accusative and infinitive after audierat; sibi is the dative governed by cedere, 'yield to her'.

sentences.t:
Non illa loco neque origine gentis
clara, sed arte fuit.
sentences.l: She was not distinguished by her place, nor by the origin of her family, but by her art.
sentences.i: It was not her home or her family's descent that made her famous, but her craft.
sentences.n: loco, origine and arte are all ablatives of respect with clara. The three ablatives stand a whole line ahead of the adjective they qualify — clara opens the following line — which is a normal Ovidian stretch.

sentences.t:
Pater huic Colophonius Idmon
Phocaico bibulas tingebat murice lanas.
sentences.l: Her father, Idmon of Colophon, used to dye thirsty wools with Phocaean purple.
sentences.i: Her father was Idmon of Colophon, who dyed absorbent wool with Phocaean purple.
sentences.n: huic is a possessive dative with pater: there is no verb 'to be' in the clause, and the dative simply marks whose father he is. Colophon and Phocaea are Ionian cities on the coast near Lydia. murex is the shellfish that yields purple dye; bibulas, 'thirsty', is of the wool drinking the dye in. The trade is a modest one, and the point of naming it is the family's rank.

sentences.t:
Occiderat mater; sed et haec de plebe suoque
aequa viro fuerat.
sentences.l: Her mother had died; but she too had been from the common people and equal to her husband.
sentences.i: Her mother was dead; she too had been common-born, of a piece with her husband.
sentences.n: aequa takes the dative viro, 'matched to her husband' — in station, not in affection. et here is 'also'. The pluperfects hold the family history behind the narrative proper.

sentences.t:
Lydas tamen illa per urbes
quaesierat studio nomen memorabile, quamvis
orta domo parva parvis habitabat Hypaepis.
sentences.l: Yet she through the Lydian cities had sought by her zeal a name to be remembered, although, sprung from a small house, she was living in small Hypaepa.
sentences.i: Yet by her devotion she had won a name worth remembering throughout the cities of Lydia, though she was born to a humble house and lived in humble Hypaepa.
sentences.n: Hypaepa was a small town below Mount Tmolus in Lydia. The repetition parva ... parvis is Ovid's own, setting the smallness of the birth against the smallness of the place. quamvis takes the indicative habitabat here, which verse allows freely.

sentences.t:
Huius ut adspicerent opus admirabile, saepe
deseruere sui nymphae vineta Timoli,
deseruere suas nymphae Pactolides undas.
sentences.l: So that they might look on her marvellous work, often the nymphs deserted the vineyards of their own Tmolus, the Pactolid nymphs deserted their own waters.
sentences.i: To gaze on her marvellous work the nymphs would leave the vineyards of their own Tmolus, and the nymphs of Pactolus their own streams.
sentences.n: deseruere is deseruerunt, the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere; it is common in Latin verse and should be read as an ordinary perfect. 'ut adspicerent' is a purpose clause with the subjunctive. Tmolus is the Lydian mountain famous for vines — the edition spells it Timolus — and Pactolus is the river famous for gold. The repeated deseruere at the head of both lines is anaphora.

sentences.t:
Nec factas solum vestes spectare iuvabat;
tum quoque, cum fierent: tantus decor adfuit arti.
sentences.l: Nor was it pleasing only to watch the finished cloths; then too, when they were being made: so great a grace was present in her art.
sentences.i: And it was not only the finished cloth that gave pleasure to watch, but the making of it too — such grace attended her craft.
sentences.n: iuvabat is impersonal, 'it was a pleasure', with the infinitive spectare as its subject. The contrast is between 'factas ... vestes', the perfect participle, the cloth already made, and 'cum fierent', the imperfect subjunctive, the cloth in the making. decor is the beauty of the doing, not of the thing done.

sentences.t:
Sive rudem primos lanam glomerabat in orbes,
seu digitis subigebat opus repetitaque longo
vellera mollibat nebulas aequantia tractu,
sentences.l: Whether she was gathering the raw wool into its first round masses, or with her fingers was working the material and softening the fleeces, gone over again and again, that matched clouds under the long drawing-out,
sentences.i: Whether she was winding raw wool into its first balls, or teasing the mass with her fingers and drawing the fleece over and over until it thinned out cloud-like under her long pull,
sentences.n: mollibat is molliebat, a syncopated imperfect that verse uses for the metre. 'nebulas aequantia' is a present participle agreeing with vellera and governing the accusative nebulas: the carded fleece 'matches clouds' for fineness. 'longo ... tractu' is an ablative of manner, the long draw of the wool between the fingers. This is the first pair of a four-part sive/seu series that runs through the stages of woolwork; the main verb comes only at the end of it.

sentences.t:
sive levi teretem versabat pollice fusum,
seu pingebat acu, scires a Pallade doctam.
sentences.l: or whether she was turning the smooth-rounded spindle with a light thumb, or was painting with the needle, you would know her taught by Pallas.
sentences.i: or spinning the smooth spindle with a light thumb, or painting with her needle — you would have known Pallas had taught her.
sentences.n: scires is a potential subjunctive addressed to an indefinite 'you': 'one would have known'. 'a Pallade doctam' is an accusative and infinitive with esse left out, and a with the ablative marks the agent. 'pingebat acu', 'she painted with the needle', is the standing Latin idiom for embroidery, and it prepares the tapestries to come.

sentences.t:
Quod tamen ipsa negat, tantaque offensa magistra
“certet” ait “mecum: nihil est, quod victa recusem.”
sentences.l: Which, however, she herself denies, and, offended at so great a teacher, she says: “let her contend with me: there is nothing that, once beaten, I would refuse.”
sentences.i: But this she denied, and, offended at being given so great a mistress, said: “Let her compete with me. There is nothing I would refuse if I lost.”
sentences.n: Quod is a connecting relative opening the sentence — 'and this she denies', not a question. negat and ait are historic presents, which quicken the pace. offensa is a perfect participle agreeing with ipsa, and 'tanta ... magistra' is the ablative of cause going with it: what offends her is being credited with a divine teacher at all. 'quod ... recusem' is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive. victa, feminine, 'having been beaten', stakes everything on the outcome.

sentences.t:
Pallas anum simulat falsosque in tempora canos
addit et infirmos, baculo quos sustinet, artus.
sentences.l: Pallas counterfeits an old woman and adds false grey hairs onto her temples, and feeble limbs, which she supports with a staff.
sentences.i: Pallas took on an old woman's shape, added false grey to her temples and frail limbs, propped on a stick.
sentences.n: simulo with a plain accusative is 'assume the likeness of'. canos is the adjective 'grey' used as a noun, 'grey hairs'. The relative clause 'baculo quos sustinet' is set inside the phrase it belongs to, between infirmos and artus — an interlacing Ovid uses constantly, and the reason for reading to the end of the line before deciding what goes with what.

sentences.t:
Tum sic orsa loqui: “Non omnia grandior aetas,
quae fugiamus, habet: seris venit usus ab annis.
sentences.l: Then she began to speak thus: “Greater age does not have everything that we should flee: experience comes from late years.
sentences.i: Then she began: “Not everything about riper age is to be shunned — experience comes with the later years.
sentences.n: 'orsa' is from the deponent ordior: passive in form, active in sense, 'she began', with est left out. 'quae fugiamus' is a relative clause of characteristic in the subjunctive, 'things of the sort we should avoid'. grandior aetas is the comparative, the age that is further on.

sentences.t:
Consilium ne sperne meum. Tibi fama petatur
inter mortales faciendae maxima lanae:
sentences.l: Do not scorn my advice. Let the greatest fame among mortals for the making of wool be sought by you:
sentences.i: Do not spurn my counsel. Seek the highest renown among mortals for the working of wool:
sentences.n: 'ne sperne', ne with the imperative, is the poetic prohibition; prose would write noli spernere or ne spernas. 'fama petatur' is a jussive subjunctive in the passive with tibi as the dative of the agent, 'let it be sought by you'. 'faciendae ... lanae' is a gerundive phrase in the genitive depending on fama, 'fame for wool that is to be worked'. The whole of the advice lies in one phrase: among mortals.

sentences.t:
cede deae veniamque tuis, temeraria, dictis
supplice voce roga: veniam dabit illa roganti.”
sentences.l: yield to the goddess and ask pardon for your words, rash girl, with a suppliant voice: she will give pardon to one who asks.”
sentences.i: give way to the goddess, reckless girl, and beg pardon for your words in a suppliant's voice: she pardons whoever asks.”
sentences.n: cedo takes the dative deae. rogo here takes the accusative of the thing asked (veniam) with the dative of what it is asked for (tuis ... dictis). temeraria is a vocative thrown into the middle of the clause. roganti is a present participle in the dative used as a noun, 'to one asking' — the pardon is conditional on the asking, and the goddess is standing there promising it about herself.

sentences.t:
Adspicit hanc torvis inceptaque fila relinquit,
vixque manum retinens confessaque vultibus iram
talibus obscuram resecuta est Pallada dictis:
sentences.l: She looks at her with grim [eyes] and abandons the threads she has begun, and scarcely holding back her hand, and having confessed her anger by her face, she answered the unrecognised Pallas with words like these:
sentences.i: She looked at her with a scowl, dropped the threads she had begun, and, barely keeping her hand off her, her face admitting her anger, she flung back at the disguised Pallas words like these:
sentences.n: torvis is an ablative plural with oculis to be supplied, which the literal marks with brackets. 'resecuta est' is from the deponent resequor: passive in form, active in sense, 'she answered back'. 'obscuram ... Pallada' is 'Pallas in the dark', that is, still unrecognised inside the old woman's shape; Pallada is the Greek accusative. 'vix manum retinens' means she can barely keep her hands off the old woman.

sentences.t:
“Mentis inops longaque venis confecta senecta.
Et nimium vixisse diu nocet.
sentences.l: “You come destitute of mind and worn out by long old age. And to have lived too long does harm.
sentences.i: “You come here witless and worn down by a long old age. And living too long does damage.
sentences.n: inops takes the genitive mentis, 'destitute of mind'. confecta is a perfect participle, feminine nominative, agreeing with the unexpressed 'you' of venis. In the second sentence the perfect infinitive 'vixisse' is the subject of nocet: the harm is not in living but in having lived so long. The line is a sententia, and it is aimed at a woman Arachne takes for a frail old crone.

sentences.t:
Audiat istas,
siqua tibi nurus est, siqua est tibi filia, voces.
sentences.l: Let her hear those words of yours, if you have any daughter-in-law, if you have any daughter.
sentences.i: Let your daughter-in-law hear talk like that, if you have one, or your daughter, if you have one.
sentences.n: istas carries contempt: 'that stuff of yours'. Audiat is jussive subjunctive. The insult works twice over — the advice is fit only for the family, and the two 'if' clauses hint that she may have neither. Note that a nurus is a son's wife, not a niece.

sentences.t:
Consilii satis est in me mihi. Neve monendo
profecisse putes, eadem est sententia nobis.
sentences.l: There is enough of counsel in me for me. And so that you may not think you have accomplished anything by advising, my judgement is the same.
sentences.i: I have counsel enough in myself, for myself. And in case you think your warning has achieved something — my mind is unchanged.
sentences.n: consilii is a partitive genitive after satis. 'in me mihi' jams an ablative of place against a dative of advantage, the two pronouns side by side so that the self-sufficiency is audible. 'neve ... putes' is a negative purpose clause; monendo is the ablative of the gerund, 'by warning'; profecisse is a perfect infinitive in indirect statement. nobis is a dative of possession, the plural used for the singular — she answers the goddess's royal plural with one of her own.

sentences.t: Cur non ipsa venit? cur haec certamina vitat?”
sentences.l: Why does she not come herself? why does she shun these contests?”
sentences.i: Why doesn't she come herself? Why does she dodge this contest?”
sentences.n: ipsa is the goddess, who is standing in front of her — the irony is the whole point of the two questions. certamina is a poetic plural for the single contest; it comes again ten lines further on.

sentences.t:
Tum dea “venit” ait, formamque removit anilem
Palladaque exhibuit.
sentences.l: Then the goddess says “she has come”, and removed the old woman's form and displayed Pallas.
sentences.i: Then the goddess said, “She has come” — and put off the old woman's shape and showed Pallas.
sentences.n: venit here is the perfect, 'she has come', not the present: the two are spelled alike and differ only in the length of the e, which this edition does not mark, and the sense decides it. The answer is a single word, and the disguise falls with it. Note the tense shift from the present ait to the perfects removit and exhibuit.

sentences.t:
Venerantur numina nymphae
Mygdonidesque nurus: sola est non territa virgo.
sentences.l: The nymphs and the Mygdonian young wives worship her divinity: the girl alone is not terrified.
sentences.i: The nymphs and the young wives of Mygdonia bowed to her godhead; the girl alone was unafraid.
sentences.n: veneror is deponent, active in sense, with numina as its accusative object. Mygdonia is a district of Phrygia, next to Lydia; these are the local women who have come to watch. virgo is Arachne. The negative sits with territa: she is the one person there not frightened.

sentences.t:
Sed tamen erubuit, subitusque invita notavit
ora rubor rursusque evanuit, ut solet aer
purpureus fieri, cum primum aurora movetur,
et breve post tempus candescere solis ab ortu.
sentences.l: But still she blushed, and a sudden redness marked her unwilling face and vanished again, as the air is wont to become purple when dawn first stirs, and after a short time to grow white from the sun's rising.
sentences.i: Yet she did blush; a sudden flush marked her face against her will and faded again, as the sky turns crimson when dawn first stirs and, a little later, whitens as the sun comes up.
sentences.n: invita is neuter plural agreeing with ora, 'her unwilling face' — it cannot go with rubor, which is masculine; the blush comes without her consent, and it is the only thing in her that yields. solet governs both infinitives, fieri and candescere. ora, literally 'mouths', is the ordinary poetic plural for a single face.

sentences.t:
Perstat in incepto stolidaeque cupidine palmae
in sua fata ruit:
sentences.l: She persists in what she has begun, and in her desire for a stupid prize she rushes into her own doom:
sentences.i: She held to her purpose, and in her craving for a foolish victory ran headlong on her own destruction.
sentences.n: 'stolidae ... palmae' — the adjective is attached to the prize, though the folly is hers: a transferred epithet. palma, the palm branch, is the prize of victory. 'in sua fata ruit' — ruo with in and the accusative, 'rush upon'; fata here is what is destined for her, which the reader can see and she cannot.

sentences.t:
neque enim Iove nata recusat,
nec monet ulterius, nec iam certamina differt.
sentences.l: for the one born of Jove does not refuse, nor does she warn further, nor does she now put off the contest.
sentences.i: For Jove's daughter did not refuse; she gave no more warnings and delayed the contest no longer.
sentences.n: 'Iove nata' is 'born from Jove', an ablative of origin standing as a periphrasis for Minerva. The three negatives, neque ... nec ... nec, drive the acceleration into the contest. certamina is again the poetic plural.

sentences.t:
Haud mora, constituunt diversis partibus ambae
et gracili geminas intendunt stamine telas
sentences.l: No delay: both take their stand in different parts and stretch twin webs with a slender warp-thread
sentences.i: No delay: the two took their places apart from each other and set up twin looms with fine warp
sentences.n: 'Haud mora' is a verbless exclamation, 'no delay', dropped in like a stage direction. constituo is used here without an object, 'take up position'. tela is the warp stretched on the loom, and so the loom itself; stamen is the warp thread, in the ablative of means. ambae, 'both', keeps the two of them exactly level for the length of the contest.

sentences.t: (tela iugo iuncta est, stamen secernit harundo);
sentences.l: (the web is fastened to the beam, a reed separates the warp);
sentences.i: (the warp is tied to the beam; a reed keeps its threads apart);
sentences.n: A parenthesis in which Ovid stops to explain the upright loom. The iugum is the cross-beam at the top from which the warp hangs; the harundo is the rod that holds alternate warp threads apart so the weft can pass between them. Three lines of technical description follow, and they are meant as description, not metaphor.

sentences.t:
inseritur medium radiis subtemen acutis,
quod digiti expediunt, atque inter stamina ductum
percusso paviunt insecti pectine dentes.
sentences.l: the weft down the middle is put in by sharp shuttles — the fingers pay it out — and, once it has been drawn between the warp-threads, the notched teeth beat it home, the comb being struck.
sentences.i: the weft that runs down the middle goes in on sharp shuttles, the fingers paying it out, and once it is drawn between the warp the notched teeth pack it tight as the reed is struck.
sentences.n: medium agrees with subtemen, which is the nominative subject of the passive inseritur: the weft that runs down the middle, between the sets of warp thread. quod is neuter and picks up subtemen, the weft, not the shuttles. 'percusso ... pectine' is an ablative absolute, 'the comb having been struck', and 'insecti ... dentes', the cut teeth, are the subject of paviunt: the weaver knocks the reed and its teeth drive the weft home.

sentences.t:
Utraque festinant cinctaeque ad pectora vestes
bracchia docta movent, studio fallente laborem.
sentences.l: Both hurry, and, girt as to their robes up to the breasts, they move their skilled arms, their eagerness beguiling the toil.
sentences.i: Both worked fast, their gowns hitched to the breast, moving practised arms, their eagerness cheating the labour.
sentences.n: utraque is singular in form but takes the plural verb festinant, and the participle cinctae is plural to match. 'cinctae ... vestes' is the Greek accusative of respect after a passive participle: 'girded as to their robes' — the robes are hitched up so the arms are free. Watch for this construction; it is not a plain accusative object. 'studio fallente laborem' is an ablative absolute: their absorption makes the work stop feeling like work.

sentences.t:
Illic et Tyrium quae purpura sensit aenum
texitur et tenues parvi discriminis umbrae,
sentences.l: There is woven both the purple that has felt the Tyrian cauldron and fine shades of small difference,
sentences.i: Into it goes purple that has known the Tyrian vat, and delicate shades barely distinct from one another,
sentences.n: The relative clause is set inside its own antecedent: 'quae purpura sensit aenum', 'the purple which has felt the cauldron', is what texitur has for its subject. sentio of the dye 'feeling' the bronze vat. Tyre in Phoenicia made the costliest purple in the ancient world. 'parvi discriminis' is a genitive of description, 'of small distinction'.

sentences.t:
qualis ab imbre solet percussis solibus arcus
inficere ingenti longum curvamine caelum:
sentences.l: such as the bow is wont, after rain, when the sunbeams are struck, to stain the long sky with its huge curve:
sentences.i: such as the rainbow that after rain, when the sunlight is caught in it, stains the long reach of the sky with its vast arc:
sentences.n: qualis is nominative, agreeing with arcus, and correlates with the umbrae just named: 'shades of the kind the rainbow makes'. 'percussis solibus' is an ablative absolute, 'the sunbeams having been struck', of the rays hitting the falling water; soles in the plural is the sun's rays. The simile runs on for three more lines and is really an argument about gradation.

sentences.t:
in quo diversi niteant cum mille colores,
transitus ipse tamen spectantia lumina fallit;
sentences.l: in which, although a thousand different colours shine, the passing-over itself nevertheless deceives the watching eyes;
sentences.i: in which, though a thousand different colours shine, the change from one to the next escapes the watching eye;
sentences.n: cum here is concessive with the subjunctive niteant, 'although they shine', and it is postponed behind the words it governs. transitus is the passage from one colour to the next. lumina, 'lights', is the standing poetic word for eyes.

sentences.t: usque adeo quod tangit idem est, tamen ultima distant.
sentences.l: to such a degree is what it touches the same, and yet the outermost parts stand apart.
sentences.i: so exactly does each shade match the one it touches — and yet the two ends are wholly unlike.
sentences.n: 'quod tangit' is 'that which it touches', each colour where it meets its neighbour. ultima is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'the extremes'. The line is a sententia that can be quoted on its own, and it is also a statement about what the two tapestries are going to do: no visible seam, and opposite ends.

sentences.t:
Illic et lentum filis inmittitur aurum
et vetus in tela deducitur argumentum.
sentences.l: There too pliant gold is sent in among the threads, and an ancient story is drawn down into the web.
sentences.i: Pliant gold too is worked in among the threads, and an old story is drawn out across the loom.
sentences.n: 'lentum ... aurum' is gold beaten out until it is flexible enough to be woven. deduco is the weaver's word for drawing thread out, and also the poet's word for spinning out a narrative, so the line describes both crafts at once. argumentum is the subject-matter of a work of art. inmittitur is the edition's spelling.

sentences.t:
Cecropia Pallas scopulum Mavortis in arce
pingit et antiquam de terrae nomine litem.
sentences.l: Pallas paints the crag of Mavors on the Cecropian citadel, and the ancient lawsuit over the land's name.
sentences.i: Pallas depicts the crag of Mars on the citadel of Cecrops, and the ancient dispute over the naming of the land.
sentences.n: Cecrops was the first king of Athens, so 'Cecropian' is Athenian and the arx is the Acropolis. 'scopulum Mavortis' is the Areopagus, the hill of Mars; Mavors is the old and grander form of the god's name. lis is a legal word, a suit at law — the quarrel over the land's name is the scene the next lines set out, and Minerva frames it as a case properly decided.

sentences.t:
Bis sex caelestes medio Iove sedibus altis
augusta gravitate sedent.
sentences.l: Twice six heavenly ones, with Jove in the middle, sit on high seats in august solemnity.
sentences.i: Twelve gods sit on high thrones, Jove in the middle, in majestic gravity.
sentences.n: 'bis sex' is twelve, the canonical council of gods, and the doubling is grander than the plain numeral. 'medio Iove' is an ablative absolute of the kind built from a noun and an adjective, with no participle in it: 'Jove being in the middle'. 'augusta gravitate' is an ablative of manner. The design begins from authority, symmetry and rank — everything Arachne's will lack.

sentences.t:
Sua quemque deorum
inscribit facies: Iovis est regalis imago.
sentences.l: His own face inscribes each of the gods: the likeness of Jove is a king's.
sentences.i: Each of the gods is labelled by his own features; Jove's likeness is kingly.
sentences.n: inscribo is 'write a title on': the face itself does the work of a written label, since a woven picture carries no names. deorum is a partitive genitive with quemque. regalis is placed last for the weight of it.

sentences.l: She makes the god of the sea stand and strike the rough rocks with his long trident, and salt water to have leapt out from the middle of the rock's wound, the pledge by which he might claim the city;
sentences.i: She shows the sea-god standing and striking the rough rock with his long trident, and salt water springing out of the middle of the rock's wound — the token by which he would claim the city;
sentences.n: facit takes an accusative and infinitive, the standing Latin way of saying what an artist has represented: 'she makes him stand'. 'deum pelagi' is Neptune. The blow of the trident is called a wound, vulnus, and the sea-water that springs from it is the salt spring shown on the Acropolis. 'quo pignore vindicet' is a relative clause of purpose with the subjunctive; vindico is the legal word for claiming a thing as one's own.

sentences.t:
at sibi dat clipeum, dat acutae cuspidis hastam,
dat galeam capiti, defenditur aegide pectus,
sentences.l: but to herself she gives a shield, gives a spear of sharp point, gives a helmet to her head; her breast is defended by the aegis,
sentences.i: To herself she gives a shield, a spear with a keen point, a helmet for her head; the aegis guards her breast.
sentences.n: sibi — she puts herself into her own picture, which is worth noticing before the tapestry that answers hers. The triple dat is anaphora, and the fourth clause breaks the pattern by turning passive, defenditur. 'acutae cuspidis' is a genitive of description. The aegis is Minerva's goatskin breastplate.

sentences.t:
percussamque sua simulat de cuspide terram
edere cum bacis fetum canentis olivae
mirarique deos: operis Victoria finis.
sentences.l: and she represents the earth, struck by her own spear-point, putting forth the offspring of the pale-grey olive with its berries, and the gods marvelling: Victory is the end of the work.
sentences.i: and she shows the earth, struck by her own spear-point, bringing forth the grey-green olive with its berries, and the gods marvelling. Victory closes the piece.
sentences.n: simulat governs two accusative-and-infinitive constructions, terram edere and deos mirari; mirari is deponent, active in sense. canentis is from caneo, 'to be grey-white', and is used of the pale underside of olive leaves. The tree is called the earth's fetus, its offspring, and it is Minerva's gift, which wins the case. The last clause has no verb at all: Victoria, capitalised, is the goddess woven in as the final figure, and finis is both the edge of the panel and the outcome of the trial.

sentences.t:
Ut tamen exemplis intellegat aemula laudis,
quod pretium speret pro tam furialibus ausis,
quattuor in partes certamina quattuor addit,
clara colore suo, brevibus distincta sigillis.
sentences.l: But so that her rival for the prize might understand from examples what reward she should expect for such frenzied acts of daring, she adds four contests into four sections, bright with their own colour, marked off by small figures.
sentences.i: But so that her rival for the honour might learn from examples what payment to look for after such mad presumption, she added four contests in the four corners, each bright in its own colour and picked out in small figures.
sentences.n: 'aemula laudis' is Arachne, the rival for the praise, with an objective genitive. 'quod pretium speret' is an indirect question with the subjunctive after intellegat. ausum is a neuter noun, 'a daring deed', here in the ablative after pro. The fourfold quattuor ... quattuor matches the four corners. sigilla are small figures. These four corner panels are a threat, and the reader should register them as one.

sentences.t:
Threiciam Rhodopen habet angulus unus et Haemum
(nunc gelidi montes, mortalia corpora quondam !),
nomina summorum sibi qui tribuere deorum.
sentences.l: One corner has Thracian Rhodope and Haemus (now cold mountains, once mortal bodies!), who assigned to themselves the names of the highest gods.
sentences.i: One corner holds Thracian Rhodope and Haemus — cold mountains now, once bodies of flesh — who took the names of the highest gods for themselves.
sentences.n: Rhodope and Haemus are Thracian mountain ranges; the story is that the pair called themselves Juno and Jupiter and were turned into the mountains they are named for. tribuere is tribuerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect. The relative qui is masculine plural although one of the two is a woman: the masculine covers a mixed pair. The exclamation and its spacing are the edition's own.

sentences.t:
Altera Pygmaeae fatum miserabile matris
pars habet: hanc Iuno victam certamine iussit
esse gruem populisque suis indicere bella.
sentences.l: The second part holds the pitiable fate of the Pygmy mother: her, beaten in a contest, Juno ordered to be a crane and to declare war on her own peoples.
sentences.i: The second panel holds the pitiable fate of the Pygmy woman, whom Juno, when she had lost the contest, ordered to become a crane and make war on her own people.
sentences.n: 'Altera ... pars' is split around the phrase it governs, an interlacing the reader meets constantly in this poem. The Pygmy queen challenged Juno and was made a crane; cranes and Pygmies were a byword for permanent war, so the punishment turns her against her own kind. 'iussit esse gruem' — iubeo with the infinitive, and the predicate gruem is accusative because it agrees with hanc.

sentences.l: She painted also Antigone, who once dared to contend with the consort of great Jove, and whom royal Juno turned into a bird;
sentences.i: She painted Antigone too, who once dared to vie with great Jove's consort, and whom royal Juno turned into a bird;
sentences.n: Antigonen is a Greek accusative. 'consorte Iovis' is Juno herself, named by her marriage rather than her name, which suits a panel warning against rivalry. ausam is from audeo, a semi-deponent: perfect in form, active in sense, 'having dared'. This Antigone is a Trojan, not the Theban one.

sentences.t:
nec profuit Ilion illi
Laomedonve pater, sumptis quin candida pennis
ipsa sibi plaudat crepitante ciconia rostro.
sentences.l: nor did Ilion help her, nor her father Laomedon, but that, with feathers taken on, she herself, a white stork, applauds herself with clattering beak.
sentences.i: Neither Troy nor her father Laomedon saved her: she took on feathers, and now, a white stork, she applauds herself with a clattering bill.
sentences.n: quin with the subjunctive after a negative clause means 'without its coming about that' — the rank did not stop the change. 'sumptis ... pennis' is an ablative absolute. Ilion is Troy, and Laomedon was its king; Antigone was his daughter. The stork's bill-clattering is turned into self-applause, so the vanity survives the transformation, which is the joke and the sting.

sentences.t: Qui superest solus, Cinyran habet angulus orbum;
sentences.l: The corner that alone is left has Cinyras bereft of his children;
sentences.i: The one corner still left holds Cinyras, robbed of his children;
sentences.n: orbus is the exact word for a parent who has lost their children, not merely 'deprived'. The relative clause stands in front of its antecedent angulus, a common poetic order — read to the comma before deciding what qui refers to. Cinyras belongs to Cyprus; Ovid gives nothing beyond the picture here, and the tale behind it is otherwise obscure.

sentences.t:
isque gradus templi, natarum membra suarum,
amplectens saxoque iacens lacrimare videtur.
sentences.l: and he, embracing the steps of a temple — the limbs of his own daughters — and lying on the stone, seems to weep.
sentences.i: and, clasping a temple's steps that are the limbs of his own daughters, lying on the stone, he seems to be weeping.
sentences.n: 'natarum membra suarum' stands in apposition to gradus: the steps are the girls' bodies, and the reader is meant to take a moment over it. videtur is the standing verb for what a work of art appears to be doing, and it keeps the whole thing at one remove — this is woven thread that seems to weep.

sentences.t:
Circuit extremas oleis pacalibus oras:
is modus est, operisque sua facit arbore finem.
sentences.l: She goes round the outermost edges with peace-bringing olive: that is the limit, and with her own tree she makes the end of the work.
sentences.i: She ran a border of peace-bringing olive round the outer edges: that was the limit she set, and with her own tree she brought the work to an end.
sentences.n: pacalis, 'of peace', from pax: the olive is the emblem of peace and Minerva's own tree, the same tree the panel has just shown her giving to Athens. modus is both the measure of the border and the restraint of the design as a whole. The composition closes on itself, which is exactly what the answering tapestry will refuse to do.

sentences.t:
Maeonis elusam designat imagine tauri
Europam: verum taurum, freta vera putares.
sentences.l: The Maeonian girl marks out Europa, tricked by the likeness of a bull: you would have thought the bull true, the waters true.
sentences.i: The Lydian girl set down Europa, deceived by the shape of a bull: you would have sworn the bull was real, the sea real.
sentences.n: Maeonis, 'the Maeonian woman', is Arachne; Maeonia is Lydia. The participle elusam ends one line and its noun Europam opens the next, holding the name back to the emphatic position. Jupiter took a bull's shape to carry Europa off over the sea. putares is a potential subjunctive addressed to an indefinite 'you', the standing formula of praise for lifelike art, matching scires earlier in this part. This opens Arachne's whole subject: the shapes gods put on, and what they did in them.

sentences.t:
Ipsa videbatur terras spectare relictas
et comites clamare suas tactumque vereri
adsilientis aquae timidasque reducere plantas.
sentences.l: She herself seemed to be gazing at the lands left behind, and to be calling her companions, and to fear the touch of the leaping water, and to draw back her frightened soles.
sentences.i: Europa herself seemed to be looking back at the land she had left, calling to her companions, shrinking from the touch of the water leaping up, pulling back her feet in fear.
sentences.n: videbatur carries four infinitives in a row, and the piling of them is what makes the woven figure move. 'comites clamare suas' — clamo with a direct object of the person called to, a poetic construction. vereri is deponent, active in sense. 'timidas ... plantas', 'frightened soles', is a transferred epithet: the fear is the girl's.

sentences.t:
Fecit et Asterien aquila luctante teneri,
fecit olorinis Ledam recubare sub alis;
sentences.l: She made Asterie also to be held by a struggling eagle, made Leda to lie back beneath a swan's wings;
sentences.i: She wove Asterie held fast by a struggling eagle, and Leda lying back under a swan's wings;
sentences.n: facio again takes an accusative and infinitive of what is represented, and here the infinitive teneri is passive: Asterie is the one held. 'aquila luctante' is a bare ablative with the passive infinitive teneri, the participle attributive to it: 'held by a struggling eagle'. The struggle belongs to the bird, that is, to the god forcing her. Some read the phrase as an ablative absolute instead, 'while the eagle struggles', which comes out at the same thing. Jupiter took the eagle's shape for Asterie and the swan's for Leda. Asterien and Ledam are Greek accusatives.

sentences.t:
addidit, ut satyri celatus imagine pulchram
Iuppiter implerit gemino Nycteida fetu,
Amphitryon fuerit, cum te, Tirynthia, cepit,
sentences.l: she added how, hidden in the likeness of a satyr, Jupiter filled the beautiful daughter of Nycteus with a twin offspring, how he was Amphitryon when he took you, woman of Tiryns,
sentences.i: she added how Jupiter, hidden in a satyr's shape, got twins on Nycteus' lovely daughter; how he was Amphitryon when he took you, lady of Tiryns;
sentences.n: 'ut ... implerit ... fuerit' are indirect questions with the perfect subjunctive, 'how he ...', all depending on addidit; the construction runs on through the next lines. Nycteida is a Greek accusative, the daughter of Nycteus — Antiope, who bore the twins Amphion and Zethus. celatus is a passive participle with an ablative of means, 'concealed by the likeness'. Tirynthia is a vocative: Ovid breaks off the report to address the woman herself, Alcmena, wife of Amphitryon, whom Jupiter came to wearing her husband's face. cepit is indicative because the cum-clause is a plain statement of when.

sentences.t:
aureus ut Danaen, Asopida luserit ignis,
Mnemosynen pastor, varius Deoida serpens.
sentences.l: how as gold he made a dupe of Danae, as fire of the daughter of Asopus, as a shepherd of Mnemosyne, as a mottled serpent of the daughter of Deo.
sentences.i: how in gold he duped Danae, in fire the daughter of Asopus, as a shepherd Mnemosyne, as a mottled snake the daughter of Deo.
sentences.n: One verb, luserit, serves all four clauses. aureus, ignis, pastor and serpens are all nominatives describing the disguised Jupiter, and each accusative is the woman; keeping that straight is the whole difficulty of the line. ludo here is 'make a dupe of'. Asopis, the daughter of the river Asopus, is Aegina; Deois, the daughter of Deo (a name of Ceres), is Proserpina. Danaen, Mnemosynen, Asopida and Deoida are all Greek accusatives. Four assaults in two lines: the compression is the argument.

sentences.t:
Te quoque mutatum torvo, Neptune, iuvenco
virgine in Aeolia posuit.
sentences.l: You too, Neptune, changed into a grim young bull, she set upon the Aeolian maiden.
sentences.i: You too, Neptune, she set in the web, turned into a fierce young bull, on the daughter of Aeolus.
sentences.n: The apostrophe turns from Jupiter to address Neptune directly, and the second person holds for the next several lines. 'mutatum ... iuvenco' uses the plain ablative of the thing one is changed into, without a preposition. The girl is Canace, daughter of Aeolus. 'virgine in Aeolia' puts the preposition between adjective and noun, a displacement verse allows freely. quoque here is the adverb 'also', not quo-que, 'and by which' — worth testing each time the word appears.

sentences.t:
Tu visus Enipeus
gignis Aloidas, aries Bisaltida fallis;
sentences.l: You, having seemed to be Enipeus, beget the Aloidae; as a ram you deceive the daughter of Bisaltes;
sentences.i: Seeming to be Enipeus, you father the Aloidae; as a ram you cheat the daughter of Bisaltes;
sentences.n: visus is from videor, 'having appeared to be'. Enipeus is a Thessalian river-god whose shape Neptune took to reach Tyro, mother of the giants Otus and Ephialtes, the Aloidae. Bisaltis, the daughter of Bisaltes, is Theophane. The verbs go into the present tense here and stay in the second person: the catalogue is being said to the god's face.

sentences.t:
et te flava comas frugum mitissima mater
sensit equum, sensit volucrem crinita colubris
mater equi volucris, sensit delphina Melantho.
sentences.l: and the mother of the crops, golden as to her hair, gentlest of all, felt you a horse; the mother of the winged horse, tressed with snakes, felt you a bird; Melantho felt you a dolphin.
sentences.i: and the golden-haired mother of the harvests, gentlest of all, knew you as a stallion; the snake-tressed mother of the winged horse knew you as a bird; Melantho knew you as a dolphin.
sentences.n: 'flava comas' is a Greek accusative of respect after an adjective, 'golden as to her hair'; 'frugum mitissima mater' is Ceres. 'crinita colubris', 'tressed with snakes', identifies the mother of the winged horse as Medusa, mother of Pegasus. Melantho is the third of them, and the dolphin is the shape she meets him in; the traditions about her are thin and Ovid gives nothing further. Each clause is te plus a predicate accusative of the shape: sentio here is of a woman experiencing the god in the form he wore, and the threefold sensit hammers the point. Neptune is still the 'you'.

sentences.t:
Omnibus his faciemque suam faciemque locorum
reddidit.
sentences.l: To all these she gave back both their own appearance and the appearance of the places.
sentences.i: To all of them she gave their own likeness and the likeness of their settings.
sentences.n: reddo is the word for an artist rendering a likeness — giving back what is there. The doubled -que ... -que is the poetic 'both ... and'. his is a dative plural picking up every figure named so far. The line insists that all of it is recognisable: no god in this web is disguised from the viewer.

sentences.l: There is Phoebus in a countryman's likeness, and how he wore now a hawk's feathers, now a lion's hide, how as a shepherd he made a dupe of Isse, daughter of Macareus;
sentences.i: There is Phoebus in a countryman's guise, and how he wore now a hawk's plumage, now a lion's skin, and how as a shepherd he duped Isse, Macareus' daughter;
sentences.n: agrestis is the genitive of the noun agrestis, 'a countryman', with imagine: 'in a countryman's likeness'. The ut-clauses are indirect questions with perfect subjunctives, gesserit and luserit, carried on from the sense of showing that runs through the whole description. 'terga leonis' is a poetic plural for the lion's hide. Macareis, the daughter of Macareus, is Isse; Macareida and Issen are Greek accusatives. luserit is the same verb used of Jupiter's deceptions in this part.

sentences.t:
Liber ut Erigonen falsa deceperit uva,
ut Saturnus equo geminum Chirona crearit.
sentences.l: how Liber deceived Erigone with a false grape, how Saturn as a horse begot the double-formed Chiron.
sentences.i: how Bacchus deceived Erigone with a counterfeit grape, and how Saturn, in horse-shape, fathered the two-natured Chiron.
sentences.n: Liber is Bacchus, and the disguise is a bunch of grapes. equo is the plain ablative of the shape taken, as with Neptune above; geminus is of Chiron's double nature, man and horse, which is the direct consequence of the shape his father wore. crearit is creaverit, a syncopated perfect subjunctive. Some editions omit the Erigone line altogether.

sentences.t:
Ultima pars telae, tenui circumdata limbo,
nexilibus flores hederis habet intertextos.
sentences.l: The last part of the web, surrounded by a fine border, has flowers interwoven with knotted ivy.
sentences.i: The outermost part of the web, edged with a fine border, has flowers woven in among linked ivy.
sentences.n: 'nexilibus ... hederis' is an ablative: ivy that knots itself as it climbs. It is Bacchus's plant, and it claims no authority over anything — set beside the olive border of the other web, which was both the emblem of peace and the goddess's own title to the city. flores ... intertextos is the accusative object of habet.

sentences.t:
Non illud Pallas, non illud carpere Livor
possit opus.
sentences.l: Not Pallas, not Envy could find fault with that work.
sentences.i: Neither Pallas nor Envy could fault that work.
sentences.n: possit is a potential subjunctive, 'could'. carpo is literally 'pluck at', and it is the ordinary word for picking holes in someone's work. Livor, 'Spite', is personified and capitalised by the edition. The verdict is the narrator's, not the goddess's — and it is the reason for what she does next.

sentences.t:
Doluit successu flava virago
et rupit pictas, caelestia crimina, vestes.
sentences.l: The golden-haired warrior maiden grieved at her success and tore the painted cloths, the crimes of the heavens.
sentences.i: The golden-haired warrior maiden was stung by Arachne's success and tore the pictured cloth — the crimes of the gods.
sentences.n: 'caelestia crimina' stands in apposition to vestes: the cloth simply is the gods' crimes, and crimen carries both the charge and the offence charged. successu is an ablative of cause — she is hurt by Arachne's succeeding, not by her failing. virago is a woman of a warrior's force. Nothing in the text says the tapestry was faulty; it says the opposite.

sentences.t:
Utque Cytoriaco radium de monte tenebat,
ter quater Idmoniae frontem percussit Arachnes.
sentences.l: And as she was holding a shuttle from the Cytorian mountain, three times, four times she struck the forehead of Idmonian Arachne.
sentences.i: And since she had a shuttle of Cytorian boxwood in her hand, three and four times she struck the brow of Arachne, Idmon's daughter.
sentences.n: 'ut ... tenebat' with the indicative is temporal, 'as she was holding it'; the circumstance is what puts the weapon in her hand. Mount Cytorus in Paphlagonia was famous for boxwood, of which shuttles were made, so Ovid names the wood by naming the mountain. 'Idmoniae ... Arachnes' is a Greek genitive; Idmon was named as her father at the start of this part. 'ter quater' without a connective — the commoner form is terque quaterque — is an idiomatic intensifier, 'again and again', not a count.

sentences.t:
Non tulit infelix laqueoque animosa ligavit
guttura.
sentences.l: The unhappy girl did not bear it, and, high-spirited, she bound her throat with a noose.
sentences.i: The wretched girl could not bear it and, too proud to yield, tied a noose round her throat.
sentences.n: fero here is of enduring an injury. animosa keeps the pride in place even at this point: the same spirit that issued the challenge does this. guttura is a poetic plural for the one throat. Ovid gives the suicide one line and a single word of the next, and does not slow down for it.

sentences.t:
Pendentem Pallas miserata levavit
atque ita “vive quidem, pende tamen, improba” dixit:
sentences.l: Pallas, having pitied her as she hung, lifted her, and said thus: “Live, indeed — but hang, all the same, you shameless thing:
sentences.i: Pallas took pity on her as she hung and lifted her, and said: “Live then — but hang, all the same, you shameless thing:
sentences.n: miserata is from the deponent miseror, active in sense, 'having pitied'. 'vive quidem, pende tamen' puts the mercy and the sentence in one breath, and the whole of it turns on pendere, which is hanging by a rope and, for what she is about to become, hanging by a thread. improba is the goddess's word and a hard one — shameless, past restraint — and the reader should hear it as her judgement, not the poem's.

sentences.t:
“lexque eadem poenae, ne sis secura futuri,
dicta tuo generi serisque nepotibus esto.”
sentences.l: and let the same law of punishment, so that you may not be free of care about the future, be pronounced for your stock and for your late descendants.”
sentences.i: and let this same sentence be laid down for your kin and for your descendants far off, so that you may never feel safe about what is coming.”
sentences.n: esto is the future imperative of sum, the form used in laws and formal decrees: the goddess is speaking like a statute, and 'dicta ... esto' means 'let it stand pronounced'. 'secura futuri' — securus with the genitive, 'free of care about'; futuri is the neuter participle used as a noun, 'what is to come'. The sentence is passed on a whole race, which is what makes it an aetiology and not merely a punishment.

sentences.t:
Post ea discedens sucis Hecateidos herbae
sparsit;
sentences.l: After these things, as she was leaving, she sprinkled her with the juices of a herb of Hecate;
sentences.i: Then, as she left, she sprinkled her with the juices of a herb of Hecate;
sentences.n: spargo takes the ablative of the thing sprinkled, with the person left to be understood. Hecateidos is a Greek genitive: the herb belongs to Hecate, goddess of witchcraft and poisons. The transformation is worked by a drug, not by a word — the goddess turns her back and walks away while it happens.

sentences.t:
et extemplo tristi medicamine tactae
defluxere comae, cum quis et naris et aures,
sentences.l: and at once, touched by the grim drug, her hair flowed away, and with it both nose and ears,
sentences.i: and at once, at the touch of the grim drug, her hair fell away, and with it nose and ears,
sentences.n: defluxere is defluxerunt, the poetic third-plural perfect. 'tactae ... comae' — the participle agrees with comae, the hair being what the drug touches; 'tristi medicamine' is the ablative of means. 'cum quis' is cum quibus, the older ablative plural of qui: 'along with which'. The change is itemised part by part, and the parts are the ones that make a face.

sentences.t: fitque caput minimum, toto quoque corpore parva est:
sentences.l: and her head becomes tiny, and in her whole body too she is small:
sentences.i: her head becomes tiny, and she is shrunken in her whole body too:
sentences.n: fit is from fio, 'becomes', which serves as the passive of facio. 'toto ... corpore' is an ablative of respect. quoque here is the adverb 'also' — worth checking every time, since the same letters can be quo-que, 'and with which'.

sentences.t:
in latere exiles digiti pro cruribus haerent,
cetera venter habet:
sentences.l: on her side slender fingers cling in place of legs, the belly holds the rest:
sentences.i: slender fingers cling at her side in place of legs; the belly takes up all the rest.
sentences.n: 'pro cruribus', 'instead of legs': the human fingers are left doing the work of a spider's legs, and that is the exact hinge of the transformation. cetera is a neuter plural used as a noun, 'everything else', and it is the object of habet. The body is described from outside, as one would look at a spider.

sentences.t:
de quo tamen illa remittit
stamen et antiquas exercet aranea telas.
sentences.l: yet out of it she sends forth the thread, and as a spider she works the ancient webs.
sentences.i: yet out of it she lets down her thread, and as a spider she plies the old webs still.
sentences.n: 'de quo' is a connecting relative picking up venter, 'and out of this'. stamen is the warp-thread of the loom and telae the weaver's webs — both words were used of her human weaving earlier in this part, so the craft is unchanged and only the weaver is. antiquas means the work she practised before. The word aranea, 'spider', is held back to the last line of the tale, where it stands in the place her name would have had.
